turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm glad you could make it in today. What brings you to see me?
turns.patient_response:
Well, doc, to be honest, I’m mostly here because people just keep getting on my case lately. It’s... well, everyone keeps saying I’m not listening to them. And it’s causing a whole lot of grief, let me tell you. 

Like, I work on the production line, right? And my supervisor, he’ll come over to my station and start explaining a new parts run or a shift change or whatever, and he is talking straight to me. Looking right in my eyes. And I’m looking right back at him! But then, I don't know, a minute later he finishes up and walks off, and I realize I only caught maybe half of what he just said. If that. So then I have to go chase him down and ask him to say it all over again, which he absolutely hates. He thinks I don't care about the job. 

And it’s not just work, it’s at home, too. My wife will be sitting right across the table telling me something important about the bills or her day, and it just... slips right past me. I have to ask her to repeat herself constantly, and she gets so mad. She thinks I’m ignoring her on purpose or tuning her out, but I swear I’m not. I just don't catch it all. It’s causing all these fights at home, and I'm getting chewed out at the plant, so... yeah, that's why I'm here. I just can't keep making everybody say everything twice, you know? It's driving everyone crazy, and it's driving me crazy too.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly states that both his supervisor and his wife complain that he is not listening when they speak directly to him, and he frequently has to ask them to repeat themselves.

turns.doctor_question: When people are speaking to you, do their words physically sound muffled or difficult to hear clearly?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, it’s definitely not that. My ears work just fine. Actually, it’s funny you ask that, because they do these mandatory hearing tests at the plant every single year—you know, OSHA regulations and all that, because the stamping presses on the floor get so incredibly loud and the company wants to make sure nobody’s going deaf on their watch. They pull you off the line, stick you in this tiny little soundproof booth, put these heavy headphones on you, and you have to press a little clicker every time you hear a beep, even the really high-pitched quiet ones. And I ace it every single time. The occupational nurse, Brenda, she always tells me I’ve got the hearing of a twenty-year-old. So physically? Physically I can hear a pin drop. 

It’s not like people sound like they’re underwater or mumbling or anything like that. When my supervisor is talking to me, his voice is loud and clear. And my wife, well, let me tell you, when she’s getting upset with me about this whole situation, she is crystal clear. There is absolutely no mistaking the sound of her voice, especially when she raises it. It’s more just... I don't know how to explain it exactly. The sound goes right into my ears perfectly fine, but then it’s like... my brain just forgets to hit the record button. I hear the noise they're making, I know they are speaking perfectly good English to me, but the actual meaning of the words just evaporates into thin air before I can grab onto it. So, yeah, no, my hearing is a hundred percent fine. It’s just whatever happens after the sound gets in there that’s giving me all this grief.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient describes that when people speak directly to him, he hears the sound but his brain fails to process or retain the meaning of their words, indicating difficulty listening.

turns.doctor_question: {"intent": "Determine whether the difficulty processing information is specific to spoken language or also affects reading written material", "question": "Do you have the same trouble understanding or retaining information
turns.patient_response:
Well, doc, to be honest with you, I don't really know? I mean, I haven't really noticed it being an issue, but then again, I don't read a whole lot of books or anything these days. Back in high school, sure, they made us read all those thick paperbacks, and I got through them alright, I guess. But nowadays? I'm not exactly sitting down in an armchair with a novel after a ten-hour shift on the line. 

Most of what I read is just, you know, the sports scores on my phone, or maybe the safety bulletins they pin up on the corkboard in the breakroom. You know the ones—they always use that bright neon yellow paper so you can't possibly miss them, usually talking about "days since the last recordable injury" or some new safety protocol for the forklift drivers in the warehouse. I can read those just fine, I think. I mean, the nice thing about reading is that it's right there in front of you, right? So if I read a sentence and it doesn't stick, I can just look at the paper again and reread it. It's not like when my supervisor talks and the words just vanish into thin air the second they leave his mouth. With paper, the words stay put. 

But then again, if it's a really long email from corporate or a big thick operating manual for a new stamping press... man, I usually just skim it or ask one of the other guys on the floor to give me the quick version. I just don't have the patience to sit there and stare at pages of text. So I couldn't tell you for sure if I have the exact same trouble with it, just because I don't do enough heavy reading for it to cause the kind of grief I'm getting with the talking. It's the face-to-face stuff that's really putting me in the doghouse with everyone.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly states that when their supervisor talks, 'the words just vanish into thin air' and notes that 'face-to-face stuff' is causing them significant trouble.
symptom_reasoning.S006: The patient admits to avoiding long emails or thick manuals, stating they 'just don't have the patience to sit there and stare at pages of text' and prefer to skim or ask others for a summary.

turns.patient_response:
Doctor, if I'm being completely honest, this isn't exactly a new thing for me. I mean, my wife and my boss are the ones on my case about it right now, but man, if you asked my mom, she'd tell you I've been like this since I was in short pants. 

I remember back in elementary school—this had to be, what, second grade? Third grade? Mrs. Gable's class, I think. Anyway, it was way before middle school. I was a nightmare for those poor teachers. They were constantly moving my desk around the room trying to find a spot where I wouldn't be a disruption. First I was in the back, then I was up front right next to the teacher's desk, then they stuck me over by the radiator, which was awful in the winter, let me tell you. But it didn't matter where they put me, because I just could not stay put in that little plastic chair. I was always up sharpening my pencil, or going to the bathroom, or just... wandering, you know? 

And the talking! Oh man, I was always getting my name on the board for calling out answers without raising my hand. The teacher would ask a math question—something simple like seven times four—and I knew it was twenty-eight, so I just yelled it out. I didn't see the point in sitting there with my hand in the air waiting to be picked when I already knew the answer. It drove them crazy. 

Plus, I was always getting into trouble for butting into what the other kids were doing. Like, if the kid next to me was working on an art project or trying to read, I'd just lean over and start talking to them or trying to help them color, even if they didn't want my help. I just had this... this motor running inside me all the time, and I couldn't keep it dialed down. So yeah, it's definitely been going on since I was a little kid. It's just that back then, I got sent to the principal's office, and now I'm getting written up by a shift supervisor. Same song, different verse, you know?

turns.doctor_question: Nowadays as an adult, do you still feel that internal restlessness or find yourself constantly fidgeting and needing to be on the move?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. I mean, I'm not running around a classroom sharpening my pencil anymore, obviously, because I'm a grown man and I'd get fired, but... the feeling itself? It hasn't gone anywhere at all. If anything, it's almost worse now because I'm an adult and I *have* to hold it in, you know? 

Like, when I'm out on the floor, I'm moving around, checking the presses, loading materials, walking the line, so I'm mostly okay. But man, you put me in one of those mandatory all-hands meetings they hold in the cafeteria every quarter? Torture. Absolute torture. They make us sit on those terrible plastic folding chairs, and the plant manager just drones on and on with his slideshow about Q3 production goals or scrap rates or whatever, and I swear... when I have to sit still like that, it feels like there's this actual, physical pressure building up inside me. 

It's hard to describe, but it starts right here in my chest, just this tight, buzzing feeling, and then it shoots right down into my legs. My legs get so restless, I'm bouncing my knee up and down, tapping my steel-toes on the linoleum, just trying to bleed off some of that energy before I explode. It literally feels like I’ve got to move or do something right that exact second or I’ll just crawl right out of my skin. 

And my wife hates it too, because even at home, if we try to sit down on the sofa and just watch a movie on a Friday night, I can't just sit there. I make it maybe fifteen minutes before that pressure starts building up again. So I'm up getting a glass of water, then I'm sitting back down, then I'm up adjusting the blinds, then I remember a squeaky hinge on the pantry door that needs WD-40, so I go grab my tools. She tells me I'm like a caged tiger pacing back and forth. But I just can't help it. If I don't keep moving, that pressure in my chest and my legs just gets to be way too much.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes bouncing his knee and tapping his feet when forced to sit still during meetings.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient frequently gets up from his seat to do other things when trying to sit down and watch a movie.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly confirms feeling intense internal physical pressure and restlessness, feeling like he will 'crawl right out of my skin' if he doesn't move.
symptom_reasoning.S013: The patient is unable to engage in a quiet leisure activity like watching a movie without getting up to perform tasks like fixing a squeaky hinge.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient constantly needs to keep moving and is described by his wife as pacing back and forth like a 'caged tiger'.
